Empirical Research Plan:  “Tax-(In)visibility and the Setting of U.S. Toll Rates”

====================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an
event-study specification.

Why appropriate?
•  Treatment (electronic toll collection, ETC) is introduced at different
   facilities in different years → natural “event” with staggered timing.  
•  Outcomes (posted tolls, traffic, revenue) are observed repeatedly before
   and after adoption → panel DID fits the research design.  
•  An event-study around the adoption date allows visual and statistical
   testing of the parallel-trends assumption and reveals dynamics.  

Secondary analyses  
•  Instrumental-variables (IV) extension: instrument the *share* of
  electronic payments with the *introduction dummy* to obtain a first-stage
  salience measure.  
•  Heterogeneous-treatment analysis by facility type, state, urbanicity, etc.

====================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Treat_it = 1 if facility i has an operational ETC system in period t
  (first full quarter after “go-live”); 0 otherwise.

Control group  
  –  Facilities that have *not yet* adopted ETC in that period.  
  –  “Never-adopters” (handful of bridges that remain cash-only) form an
     additional pure-control subsample.

Treatment timing / event date  
  Adoption date = first day ETC is accepted for at least 90 % of lanes.
  We measure time in quarters (or months if data allow):
        rel_time_it = (t – adoption_date_i)

No RDD running variable; treatment is discrete.

====================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel trends: absent ETC, treated and control facilities would have
     evolved similarly in posted toll rates (and traffic, revenue).

     Plausibility: facilities are often regulated by the same state toll
     authority; toll changes are typically synchronized across assets,
     supporting common trends.

A2.  No anticipation: policymakers do not systematically change toll rates
     in the *pre-adoption* windows *because* ETC is coming.

     Plausibility: installation periods are short and technical; public
     notification usually follows rather than precedes board votes on toll
     hikes. Pre-trend test will probe this.

A3.  No spillovers / SUTVA: ETC adoption at Facility i does not directly
     change outcomes at Facility j that has not adopted.

     Plausibility: spatially distant facilities unlikely to share traffic;
     we will verify by dropping neighbors and by using distance weights.

A4.  Exogenous timing conditional on controls: after conditioning on
     facility and state-by-year fixed effects, the exact adoption quarter is
     unrelated to unobserved shocks to toll policy.

     Plausibility: ETC roll-outs largely driven by technological readiness
     and state-level financing, not short-run revenue motives.

====================================================================
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous adoption (facilities facing fiscal stress adopt first).  
    – Include pre-adoption traffic-growth trends, maintenance spending, and
      lagged revenues as controls.  
    – Event-study pre-coefficients close to zero bolster credibility.  
    – IV robustness: instrument adoption timing with state-level
      E-ZPass-network membership or federal grants for ITS deployment.

T2. Simultaneous capital upgrades (lane expansions) that could raise tolls
    and traffic independent of salience.  
    – Collect project-level data (Federal Highway Admin. Major Projects
      list) and add explicit controls; drop quarters with major capacity
      openings.  
    – Separate analysis limited to facilities without concurrent upgrades.

T3. Traffic diversion / network spillovers.  
    – Use distance-based weights and exclude facilities within 30 km of a
      treated neighbor in robustness checks.  
    – Aggregate to *state-wide* toll-authority level as an alternative unit
      of analysis; similar results would indicate limited diversion bias.

====================================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-dimensional fixed effects DID
library(did)          # Callaway-Sant’Anna robustness
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------
tolls <- fread("us_toll_facilities_panel.csv")   # one row per facility-quarter

# 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------------
tolls[, adopt_qtr := as.Date(adoption_date)]
tolls[, rel_qtr    := as.integer((quarter_date - adopt_qtr)/90)]   # event time
tolls[, treat      := (quarter_date >= adopt_qtr)]
tolls[, post       := fifelse(treat==TRUE, 1, 0)]
tolls[, ln_toll    := log(toll_rate)]
tolls[, ln_volume  := log(traffic_volume)]
tolls[, ln_revenue := log(revenue)]

# 3. Main Spec: DID with 2-Way FE ----------------------------------
did_main <- feols(ln_toll ~ post | facility_id + quarter_date,
                  data = tolls, cluster = "facility_id")
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-Study ----------------------------------------------------
es <- feols(
  ln_toll ~ sunab(adopt_qtr, quarter_date) | facility_id + quarter_date,
  data = tolls, cluster = "facility_id")
iplot(es, ref.line = 0)          # visual check of pre-trends

# 5. Consumer-Side Outcomes ----------------------------------------
did_volume   <- feols(ln_volume  ~ post | facility_id + quarter_date,
                      data = tolls, cluster = "facility_id")
did_revenue  <- feols(ln_revenue ~ post | facility_id + quarter_date,
                      data = tolls, cluster = "facility_id")

# 6. Robustness: Facility-Specific Trends --------------------------
did_trend <- feols(
  ln_toll ~ post | facility_id + quarter_date + facility_id^time,
  data = tolls, cluster = "facility_id")

# 7. Callaway-Sant’Anna Robustness ---------------------------------
cs_out <- att_gt(yname   = "ln_toll",
                 tname   = "qtr_num",
                 idname  = "facility_id",
                 gname   = "first_treat_qtr",
                 data    = as.data.frame(tolls))
agg_effects <- aggte(cs_out, type = "simple")
summary(agg_effects)
```

====================================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: making a tax less salient reduces political resistance,
allowing authorities to set *higher* rates.  
Prior on magnitude: within three years of ETC adoption, posted tolls rise by
≈ 5–10 % relative to the counterfactual.  

Consumer response: because the charge is less visible, price elasticity of
demand falls; traffic volumes decline *less* than the price increase (say
–2 % for a 5 % price rise), so net revenue increases ≈ 3–7 %.

====================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  Clear treatment definition & timing ................. 1  
C2  Parallel trends supported by pre-period data ........ 1  
C3  No manipulation of treatment timing ................. 0.5  
C4  No spillovers or interference ........................ 0.5  
C5  Robust standard errors / inference appropriate ...... 1  
Total (max 5) = 4.0 → “mostly credible but watch endogenous timing & spillovers”

====================================================================
End of Plan
